newsitem.title: UK: Expectations for UK in EMU jump - JP Morgan.
newsitem.headline: Expectations for UK in EMU jump - JP Morgan.

text.p: The market believes there is a more than 50 percent chance Britain will join the launch of European monetary union in 1999, a leap in expectations since a week ago, according to financial prices monitored by JP Morgan.
The probability assumed by the market of Britain joining Germany and France in the first wave of EMU jumped to 53 percent from 36 the previous week.
Last Friday saw Britain's Labour Party -- widely viewed as more EMU-friendly than the Conservatives they ousted -- take power for the first time in 18 years.
JP Morgan's "EMU calculator" showed expectations of a broad-based start to currency union edging up across the board, with only Sweden bucking the trend.
Italy's assumed probability rose five points to 56, while Spain's ticked up to 71 percent from 68 the week before.
Expectations for Finland climbed to 77 percent from 74, Portugal to 73 from 72 and Ireland to 60 from 58.

Denmark -- which has now replaced Britain at the bottom of the market's EMU-expectations league -- stuck at 47 percent, unchanged from the week ending May 2. Denmark is the only other EU country to have a negotiated option on EMU membership.
The probability of Sweden participating currency union in 1999 edged down three points to 54 percent.
Swedish finance minister Erik Asbrink said on Wednesday that the government's decision on EMU must match the public view -- and polls show most Swedes are sceptical about joining in 1999.
That fuelled talk that Swedish politicians are preparing to announce that the country does not intend to join in the launch.
The U.S. investment firm's calculator showed the readings for France and Belgium remained at 100 percent.
JP Morgan points out there is a reasonable margin of error in overall probability levels of between three and five points.
The EMU calculator is derived from the interest rate swaps market.
The probabilities are derived from the actual swap spread, an in-house assumption of what the spread would be if EMU were not a factor, and the expected spread after EMU participation, which is zero.
